cards.heading: Routers
cards.body: A router connects different IP networks and forwards packets between them using its routing table. It's the boundary of a broadcast domain and usually the default gateway for the hosts on each LAN. Each router interface is its own broadcast domain. By contrast every switch port is its own collision domain, but all ports in one VLAN share a broadcast domain, and a hub puts all its ports in one collision domain.
cards.example: PC 192.168.1.10 → default gateway R1 192.168.1.1 → R1 routes to 10.5.0.0/16

cards.heading: Layer 2 and layer 3 switches
cards.body: A layer 2 switch forwards frames inside a LAN by MAC address. A multilayer (layer 3) switch also routes between VLANs in hardware using SVIs, so it can be the default gateway for many VLANs at wire speed.
cards.example:
interface vlan 10
 ip address 10.10.10.1 255.255.255.0
ip routing

cards.heading: Next-generation firewalls and IPS
cards.body: A firewall filters traffic between security zones and is stateful: it remembers outgoing sessions and lets only their return traffic back in. A next-generation firewall (NGFW) adds application awareness, user identity and an integrated IPS. An IPS sits inline and blocks traffic that matches attack signatures; an IDS only watches a copy and alerts. Because an NGFW inspects traffic up to layer 7 (application visibility and control), it can block a specific application whatever port it uses. An IDS usually gets its copy of traffic from a SPAN port.

cards.heading: Access points and wireless LAN controllers
cards.body: An access point (AP) bridges wireless clients onto the wired network. In larger networks lightweight APs are managed centrally by a wireless LAN controller (WLC), which handles configuration, security, roaming and RF tuning. Lightweight APs join the WLC over CAPWAP tunnels; the WLC tunes channels and power and handles authentication and roaming for the whole WLAN.

cards.heading: Endpoints and servers
cards.body: Endpoints are the devices people use: PCs, phones, printers, cameras and IoT sensors. Servers provide services to them, such as web, email, DNS, DHCP and file sharing. The client/server roles are about the job a device is doing, not the hardware.

cards.heading: Power over Ethernet
cards.body: PoE delivers power over the Ethernet cable from the switch (PSE, power sourcing equipment) to the device (PD, powered device) such as an AP, IP phone or camera, so no separate power outlet is needed. A switch has a total PoE budget shared by all its ports: a 370 W budget powers 370 / 30 = 12 devices at the full PoE+ 30 W, even if the switch has 24 ports.
cards.example:
802.3af PoE     15.4 W per port
802.3at PoE+    30 W
802.3bt PoE++   60 W (type 3) / 90-100 W (type 4)

cards.heading: Which layer each device works at
cards.body: Think of the highest layer a device looks at to make its decision. A hub (and a repeater) just repeats bits: layer 1. A layer 2 switch reads MAC addresses in frames: layer 2. A router reads IP addresses in packets: layer 3. A next-generation firewall can look all the way into the application: layer 7.
cards.example:
Hub ............ Layer 1  bits
Switch ......... Layer 2  frames, MAC addresses
Router ......... Layer 3  packets, IP addresses
NGFW ........... Layer 7  applications
